1.pericope_label: The burden of Tyre: the ships hear it at sea

schools.summary: Place the oracle in history and geography: Tyre is the commercial counterpart to Babylon's imperial power and closes the series against the nations, and the chapter is read against the recorded relations of Tyre with Israel and Assyria.
Read the opening wealth as material for the judgment: the trade, the island site and the Nile harvest are set out so that God's hand in the coming ruin may be the more evident.
Fix the prophecy to its fulfilments and its idiom, dating the ruin far in advance, explaining the silence as the posture of grief, and glossing Sihor and the black soil of Egypt.
Take the ships as the frame of the whole oracle, and the flourishing of Tyre as what makes her fall dismal, with the daughter city outgrowing the mother.

debates.question: Which conqueror does the oracle foretell?

positions.view: Nebuchadnezzar, denounced a hundred and twenty years before the event, the seventy years being the duration of the Babylonian empire
Alexander, who stormed the city with great difficulty
both in succession, the prophecy respecting the first directly and the second also

debates.question: What is the isle whose inhabitants are told to be silent?

positions.view: the coast, the narrow seaboard strip held by the Phoenicians
Tyre itself, which stood off the shore as an island until Alexander joined it to the mainland

outliers.reading: Alone treats the oracle structurally, pairing Tyre with Babylon as the two types of heathen pride, the one subjugating nations with an iron arm and securing its rule by deportation, the other taking their treasures as peaceably as it could and securing its advantage by colonies and factories.

themes: The burden of Tyre. Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste, so that there is no house, no entering in: from the land of Chittim it is revealed to them.
Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle; thou whom the merchants of Zidon, that pass over the sea, have replenished.
And by great waters the seed of Sihor, the harvest of the river, is her revenue; and she is a mart of nations.

4.pericope_label: Zidon shamed, the flight west, and the counsel against the crowning city

schools.summary: Recover the political and lexical detail: the strength of the sea is the rock-island, the flight to Tarshish is the farthest and hardest refuge, and the crowning city is the distributor of crowns whose merchants bear the name of Canaanites.
Hear the passage as address and question: the lament is a taunt put into Tyre's own mouth, and the demand who has taken this counsel is asked to rouse sluggish hearers before the answer names God.
Explain the figures and settle the facts: Zidon the mother city, Tyre the guard of that sea, the antiquity older than Joshua's day, and the flat verdict that this is the word of God and not of man.

debates.question: Whose lament is heard in the fourth verse?

positions.view: Zidon's, addressed as the bereaved mother city, sitting as a widow with no power to fill her streets again
Tyre's own, the words being put into her mouth as a taunt at her boast of colonies

debates.question: What does it mean that her own feet shall carry her far off?

positions.view: the inhabitants transporting the city itself from the mainland to the island, far denoting interval rather than great distance
her feet are wont to carry her, a description of her colonies rather than of exile
banishment and long wandering, made harder by the poverty that goes with it

outliers.reading: Alone leaves the ancient city for his own century, comparing the merchants of Venice who reckon themselves the equals of princes, and the factors of Antwerp who spend beyond the means of the wealthiest nobility.

themes: Be thou ashamed, O Zidon: for the sea hath spoken, even the strength of the sea, saying, I travail not, nor bring forth children, neither do I nourish up young men, nor bring up virgins.
As at the report concerning Egypt, so shall they be sorely pained at the report of Tyre.
Pass ye over to Tarshish; howl, ye inhabitants of the isle.
Is this your joyous city, whose antiquity is of ancient days? her own feet shall carry her afar off to sojourn.
Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?
The Lord of hosts hath purposed it, to stain the pride of all glory, and to bring into contempt all the honourable of the earth.

10.pericope_label: The girdle loosed, the hand over the sea, and the land of the Chaldeans

schools.summary: Read the section against Assyrian records and Phoenician usage: the colonies break free, the shaken kingdoms reach far beyond Phoenicia, Canaan stands for Phoenicia itself, and the thirteenth verse describes a siege rather than an origin.

Keep the argument on providence: the ruin of Tyre draws many kingdoms with it, requires no instrument but the expressed will of God, and is confirmed by the older example of a people who were nothing until Assyria settled them.
Work through the obscurity clause by clause, weighing manuscripts and versions, and account for the Chaldeans as a wandering people gathered into Babylon by an Assyrian founder.

debates.question: Who is the daughter of Tarshish told to overflow her land?

positions.view: Tyre herself, born of the sea and nursed by it, her people fleeing as swiftly as a river runs
Tarshish the colony, now spreading in independent action because the mother city restrains her no longer

debates.question: What is the girdle that is loosed?

positions.view: a mound or dam, the ruined city being a river whose banks are broken and whose waters are wasted
the ditches, mounds, ramparts and sea that fortified the city on every side
the supremacy of Tyre, the tribute and limits she imposed on her colonies

debates.question: What does the thirteenth verse say of the Chaldeans?

positions.view: that they were once no people, a rude wandering tribe of no account until an Assyrian king gathered and settled them, and afterwards overthrew their founders
that this people is no more, Asshur having given it to the desert beasts, the towers being Assyrian siege-works against Babylon and the palaces those of the besieged

outliers.reading: Alone notes that Phoenicia called itself Kena'an, and that this is the only place in the Old Testament where the name is narrowed so far, the shaken kingdoms being the whole of western Asia and Egypt summoned as instruments of destruction.

themes: Pass through thy land as a river, O daughter of Tarshish: there is no more strength.
He stretched out his hand over the sea, he shook the kingdoms: the Lord hath given a commandment against the merchant city, to destroy the strong holds thereof.
And he said, Thou shalt no more rejoice, O thou oppressed virgin, daughter of Zidon: arise, pass over to Chittim; there also shalt thou have no rest.

Behold the land of the Chaldeans; this people was not, till the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness: they set up the towers thereof, they raised up the palaces thereof; and he brought it to ruin.
Howl, ye ships of Tarshish: for your strength is laid waste.

15.pericope_label: Seventy years, the harlot's song, and merchandise made holy

schools.summary: Measure the number and the figure: the seventy years are read as a fixed or symbolic term rather than a reign, the song is the harlot's known lyric, and the closing gift is traced to proselytes, to Persian-age commerce and to Tyrian help at the second temple.

Take the harlot as the trade itself, honest in principle but full of fraud in practice, and read the mercy in two stages, the restoring of the city and then the consecrating of her gains to the household of faith.

Tie the seventy years to the captivity and the royal race of Nebuchadnezzar, follow the city's later fortunes down to its ruin, and take the last verse as a plain prophecy of the conversion of the Tyrians.

Set adversity and prosperity over against each other so that no city may presume or despair, and turn the closing verse on the reader, who is to lay out his gains in piety and charity rather than hoard them.

debates.question: What are the days of one king by which the seventy years are measured?

positions.view: the span of one kingdom, from Nebuchadnezzar's first conquests to the taking of Babylon by Cyrus
one royal race, that of Nebuchadnezzar, ending in his son's son
a fixed and unchangeable period determined by a single sovereign will, no reign of that length being on record
the ordinary age of a man, a king being named because Tyre reckoned her years by her king's life

debates.question: How far does the last verse go?

positions.view: to the conversion of the Tyrians and the consecrating of their gains to God
to the admission of proselytes and the renewal of the old alliance with Judah, reversing the law that barred such gifts from the sanctuary
not to conversion but to something approaching it, a profane trade made subservient to a holy purpose

outliers.reading: Alone carries the city's history past the prophecy, through its early Christianity and fourteen bishoprics, the Saracen conquest, the Christian recovery, the Mamelukes and the Turks, down to a bare rock fit only for spreading nets upon.

themes: And it shall come to pass in that day, that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, according to the days of one king: after the end of seventy years shall Tyre sing as an harlot.
Take an harp, go about the city, thou harlot that hast been forgotten; make sweet melody, sing many songs, that thou mayest be remembered.

And it shall come to pass after the end of seventy years, that the Lord will visit Tyre, and she shall turn to her hire, and shall commit fornication with all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth.

And her merchandise and her hire shall be holiness to the Lord: it shall not be treasured nor laid up; for her merchandise shall be for them that dwell before the Lord, to eat sufficiently, and for durable clothing.
